extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, industrialists, and legal/economic readers concerned with patents, manufacturing policy, and exportation of machinery
extracted.subtask_description: Expository analysis of patent/copyright law and the policy arguments for and against restricting the exportation of machinery, with attention to industrial organization, capital mobility, and the role of science in manufactures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents secure fabrication to inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of patents secures to inventors the fabrication of their invention, because no competitors can derive a profit from invading a patent so exercised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents provide exclusivity that enables an inventor to realize returns on invention-related capital and effort; this is the principal justification for patent protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright allied to patents but must balance knowledge advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright law is allied to patent law; though infringement is often straightforward to decide, the current law can in some cases produce considerable hardship and impede the advancement of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation protecting literary and intellectual creations should avoid producing undue hardship or unnecessary impediments to the dissemination and development of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit limited partnerships to mobilize capital for inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing limited partnerships (where some partners' liability is limited) can aid division of labour and enable persons of moderate capital, who are good judges of inventions, to fund inventive workmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited partnerships could match capital with inventive labor, restrain impractical projects, supply judicious funding, and provide profit opportunities for capital-providing partners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on workmen leaving the country are unjust and ineffective
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws forbidding workmen to go out of the country are at variance with liberty, tend to be inefficient in practice, and were repealed after proving ineffectual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such migration restrictions are difficult to enforce (workers can disguise themselves), may deter return by fear of punishment, and thus fail to achieve intended protectionist aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibiting machinery export sacrifices machine-makers for machine-users
rubrics_metrics.description: A prohibition on exporting machinery sacrifices the interests of the makers of machinery for those who merely use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Export bans were justified as preventing foreign adoption of improved machinery, but they impose a cost on the domestic class that manufactures machines, potentially reducing innovation and scale in that sector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing success depends on factory economy as well as machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: To succeed in a manufacture it is necessary not merely to possess good machinery, but that the domestic economy of the factory should be most carefully regulated (division of labour, organization, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing competitive advantage or consequences of exporting machinery, consider organization, division of labour, skill, and factory practices alongside the hardware itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess foreign competitive threat by human and institutional factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if identical machinery were available abroad, deficiencies in arrangement of work, division of labour, skill and perseverance of workmen, enterprise of masters, and lack of capital will keep foreigners behind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and risk assessments should weigh institutional/cultural/organizational advantages (habit, incremental experience, supporting capital) not just possession of machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exported machinery may often be already superseded
rubrics_metrics.description: If exportation were permitted, exports would often consist of tools and machines already superseded by new inventions, which could be detrimental to the trade and manufactures of the importing country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting export may lead to the sale of obsolete equipment abroad; regulators and exporters should consider whether machines offered are current or superseded and the consequences for foreign customers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-makers prefer home orders and price foreign sales higher
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine-makers generally prefer domestic orders and commonly charge foreign customers an additional price (estimated five to twenty-five percent) because of installation, sending skilled men abroad, risk of talent loss, and higher repair costs abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Export pricing reflects after-sales service needs, risk of losing skilled personnel, and higher liability/repair exposure; these commercial practices shape the practical effects of exportation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free exportation of machinery will enlarge skilled machine-making class
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing free export of machinery would increase the class of skilled machine-makers, raise wages in that skilled class, and potentially enable England to supply the world with machinery to mutual advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy permitting exports can stimulate a domestic machinery-making sector, create durable employment for skilled workers, and produce long-term national advantages even if some manufacturing users decline in number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign purchase of machines will not halt future demand due to continuous improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unlikely foreign purchase of existing machines will stop demand for new machines because machinery is subject to continual improvement and supersession, sustaining ongoing demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The usual progression of improvements and the rate at which machines are superseded mean exporters can expect repeat demand as customers adopt new inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume a universal limit of perfection for all machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: While individual species of machinery may approach a limit of perfection, it is impossible that all kinds of mechanism have reached their ultimate limit; improvements usually continue, especially where large numbers of machines are employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and business planning should allow for continued incremental innovation across many branches rather than presuming universal technological stagnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exportation facilitates transfer of capital and sale of obsolete machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting export would create foreign demand for machinery, enabling capitalists to sell old machinery more readily and transfer capital to more advantageous employments; exporters could also use foreign markets to dispose of superseded equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening export markets increases capital mobility, lowers the loss on liquidation of machinery-intensive investments, and eases adoption of new improvements by manufacturers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liquidity and resale value of assets influence the mobility of capital and profit rates
rubrics_metrics.description: The ease with which capital can be transferred between employments (depends on how much is realizable by sale of assets like machinery) has an important effect on comparative rates of profit and investment decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing trades or investments, account for the resale value of specialized assets and the loss in removing capital; low realizable value constrains capital mobility even if nominal profit rates differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate foreign competition risk by transport, infrastructure, and resource costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquiries into injury from foreign competition should consider facilities of transport, the existing mass of capital in roads/canals/machinery, and resource costs (e.g., price of iron and fuel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive advantage arises from infrastructure and input-cost differentials; policy assessments must include geographic and infrastructural factors, not only manufacturing techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid conveyance increases a country's productive power
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements in modes of conveyance (e.g., railroads) save time for travelers and workers; time savings are equivalent to additions to the productive power of the country without increasing food consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investing in transport infrastructure yields productivity dividends by effectively increasing available working time, particularly for more valuable classes of workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufactures increasingly require intimate connexion with science
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts and manufactures are intimately connected with the progress of the severer sciences; applied sciences derive facts from experiment, but their utility depends on reasonings from abstract science, and improvement requires combined exertions of theorists and practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industrial advancement demands collaboration between theoretical scientists and practical engineers/workmen, and policies should foster such integration (division of mental labour applied to industry).

rubrics_metrics.name: State should support and compensate cultivators of abstract science
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of great principles often requires devoted minds, costly apparatus, and time incompatible with ordinary professions; it is fit for the state to consider compensating such cultivators for sacrifices they endure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public policy ought to provide encouragement, honors, or material support to scientific professionals so that abstract science—essential to applied improvements—is not neglected or driven abroad.
